These tests exercise actual enforcement within a stated boundary.

questions.objective: Derive measurable security requirements from function, consequence and operating mode.
questions.prompt: A containment rule blocks a malicious command and removes the only required alarm channel. Which result applies?
options: Alarm availability can be ignored during any security incident.
Security enforcement passed, but integrated service acceptance failed.
The whole system passed because the command was blocked.
explanations: Operational consequences and approved continuity arrangements still matter.
Both security and required operational function must be evaluated.
One control result does not close the service requirement.

questions.objective: Separate risk treatment, security levels, safety integrity and assurance evidence.
questions.prompt: Who should accept a documented residual risk affecting facility service?
options: The accountable risk owner using the engineering evidence and authority model.
Whichever learner scores highest in the quiz.
The firewall automatically when a rule compiles.
explanations: Acceptance belongs to the authorised accountable owner.
Knowledge assessment grants no organisational authority.
Syntax validation cannot make a risk decision.

questions.objective: Construct a requirements-to-test crosswalk with explicit ownership and residual risk.
questions.prompt: A standards register cites “IC34” as the sole normative requirement. What is missing?
options: The IC34 course completion date alone.
A supplier certificate without its evaluated scope.
The applicable licensed standard part, publisher, edition, requirement and boundary.
explanations: A training date does not identify applicable normative clauses.
Supplier certification does not establish the installation’s complete applicable requirements.
A course identifier is not a normative clause.

questions.objective: Reconcile physical, logical, software, firmware and identity inventories with confidence and provenance.
questions.prompt: Four host addresses and four BMC addresses belong to four servers. How should inventory represent them?
options: Four physical assets with eight related interfaces.
Eight physical servers.
Only the host addresses because BMCs are not relevant.
explanations: Interfaces and assets are different entities.
Address count does not establish physical count.
BMC authority and firmware are in scope.

questions.objective: Choose safe discovery methods and document coverage blind spots.
questions.prompt: A silent serial controller is missing from a passive IP capture. What is justified?
options: It is definitely decommissioned.
The entire production subnet may be scanned without approval.
Its presence remains unresolved by that capture; use gateway records and authorised physical or point verification.
explanations: Silence is not proof of removal.
A visibility gap does not grant testing authority.
The observation has a defined blind spot.

questions.objective: Trace attack paths from entry conditions to authority and operational consequence.
questions.prompt: Two segmented server groups share one BMC administrator and backup account. What matters most?
options: Redundant uplinks eliminate the shared credential risk.
Shared authority can create a common compromise and recovery failure path.
Segmentation proves complete independence.
explanations: Link redundancy does not separate administrative or recovery authority.
Identity and recovery dependencies cross network boundaries.
Network separation alone does not separate authority.

questions.objective: Reconcile physical, logical, software, firmware and identity inventories with confidence and provenance.
questions.prompt: Which two fields help reconcile conflicting inventory observations? Select two.
options: Source and observation time.
Stable physical identity and replacement history.
The most recent source overwrites all conflicting fields automatically.
explanations: Provenance helps explain timing and method differences.
Stable identity links interface and hardware changes.
Recency alone does not resolve identity changes or source-specific blind spots.

questions.objective: Trace attack paths from entry conditions to authority and operational consequence.
questions.prompt: A risk report says “attacker reaches TCP port, therefore controller logic changed.” What evidence is missing?
options: A transport-layer packet capture showing connection establishment.
A generic vulnerability score for the operating system.
Application permission, required authentication and demonstrated action semantics.
explanations: A connection trace still does not prove application permission or process action.
A general score does not validate this specific authority edge.
Reachability does not prove authority or control action.

questions.objective: Choose safe discovery methods and document coverage blind spots.
questions.prompt: A planned active discovery test lacks service monitors and stop conditions. What is the correct disposition?
options: Disable protective controls to avoid interruptions.
Hold until scope, operational controls and restoration prerequisites are defined.
Proceed because the tool is common in IT.
explanations: Independent protections must be retained.
A safe authorised test needs explicit operational boundaries.
Tool familiarity does not prove OT compatibility.

questions.objective: Separate authentication, authorisation and accountability across human, device and service identities.
questions.prompt: An operator cannot see a firmware-update button but can call the update API successfully. What failed?
options: Only the directory password policy.
The operator’s ability to authenticate.
Authorisation at the API boundary.
explanations: The accepted forbidden API action shows an authorisation failure regardless of password policy.
The scenario shows authentication succeeded; privilege enforcement is the issue.
The forbidden action is still accepted.

questions.objective: Test certificate enrolment, expiry, revocation and trust dependencies.
questions.prompt: A TLS session validates successfully. Which additional fact still needs verification?
options: Whether every user now needs no role checks.
Whether the authenticated identity may perform the requested control action.
Whether encryption automatically calibrated the sensor.
explanations: Application authorisation remains necessary.
Transport trust and application permission are separate.
Cryptography does not establish measurement correctness.

questions.objective: Design emergency and recovery authority that preserves least privilege after restoration.
questions.prompt: Restoring yesterday’s directory returns a departed vendor account. What is required before acceptance?
options: Apply the independently retained revocation record and retest denied actions.
Accept because the restore completed without errors.
Delete the entire recovery log.
explanations: Restoration must preserve removed authority.
A successful restore job does not prove secure authority.
Deleting records removes evidence without fixing access.

questions.objective: Test certificate enrolment, expiry, revocation and trust dependencies.
questions.prompt: Which two conditions belong in a certificate lifecycle test? Select two.
options: Unavailable time or certificate-status dependencies.
Only successful authentication with a currently valid certificate.
Expired or revoked credentials.
explanations: Dependency loss can change validation behaviour.
A valid-certificate success does not exercise expiry, revocation or dependency loss.
These exercise trust termination.

questions.objective: Separate authentication, authorisation and accountability across human, device and service identities.
questions.prompt: A service account has no owner because it is automated. What is the strongest correction?
options: Remove all logging to protect the secret.
Assign ownership, bounded permissions and tested secret rotation.
Give it permanent domain administration.
explanations: Logs can record activity without exposing secrets.
Unattended identity still needs lifecycle control.
Broad privilege increases consequence.

questions.objective: Design emergency and recovery authority that preserves least privilege after restoration.
questions.prompt: The normal vault and emergency credential both require the failed directory. What does this reveal?
options: An unresolved common recovery dependency.
Independent recovery by definition.
A reason to remove authentication permanently.
explanations: Both routes fail together.
A different label does not create independence.
Permanent bypass sacrifices required control.

questions.objective: Derive zone and conduit policy from function, trust and consequence.
questions.prompt: An engineer labels every VLAN a security zone without documenting trust or flows. What is missing?
options: An assumption that routed boundaries eliminate shared administrative authority.
Security requirements and controlled communications derived from function and consequence.
A one-to-one mapping from VLAN tags to organisational departments.
explanations: Routing does not by itself separate privileged identities or recovery dependencies.
Zones and conduits express security boundaries, not just tags.
Department labels do not establish security requirements or every cross-boundary path.

questions.objective: Validate approved and denied application flows across normal and degraded paths.
questions.prompt: A firewall permits a protocol port for both readers and engineers. What proves that readers cannot write?
options: A supported application permission and a negative write test.
A successful ping from the reader.
The port number alone.
explanations: Operation-level enforcement must be demonstrated where it exists.
Ping cannot establish application authorisation.
One port may carry several operations.

questions.objective: Assess containment, remote access and management dependencies without defeating required service.
questions.prompt: A vendor session remains usable after its approved window closes. Which acceptance criterion failed?
options: Only an accounting-record retention requirement.
Only the vendor’s ability to reach the login portal.
Effective termination of temporary authority.
explanations: The session can still perform an action, so effective authorisation termination failed.
The failure concerns retained target authority after expiry, even if portal reachability is expected.
The target can still exercise expired access.

questions.objective: Validate approved and denied application flows across normal and degraded paths.
questions.prompt: Which two observations are needed after firewall failover? Select two.
options: Both appliances report a healthy hardware state.
Approved application flows and fresh data still work.
Denied actions remain denied and are observable.
explanations: Hardware health alone does not demonstrate failover application service and policy enforcement.
Availability must be checked at the application.
Security enforcement must survive the transition.

questions.objective: Assess containment, remote access and management dependencies without defeating required service.
questions.prompt: Proposed containment removes the only alarm path for an active process. What should happen before execution?
options: Assess the operational consequence and approve a tested continuity arrangement.
Assume isolation is always safest.
Turn off independent equipment protections.
explanations: Containment must preserve or deliberately manage required function.
The safe response depends on the actual process.
Security response does not authorise defeating protection.

questions.objective: Derive zone and conduit policy from function, trust and consequence.
questions.prompt: A tenant cannot reach the data VLAN but can administer its firewall. What has the design missed?
options: The application data-retention schedule.
The permitted size of tenant broadcast domains.
The management-plane trust boundary.
explanations: Retention matters separately but does not close the management bypass.
Broadcast-domain sizing does not remove firewall administrative authority.
Administrative access can change the enforcing policy.

questions.objective: Build a supported hardening baseline across host, controller, firmware and application layers.
questions.prompt: A host patch report is current, but the BMC firmware is unrecorded. What is justified?
options: Host patch status is known; management-firmware assurance remains open.
The whole platform is fully hardened.
BMC firmware is outside infrastructure security.
explanations: Different layers need their own evidence.
One layer cannot establish every other layer.
The charter explicitly includes BMC and firmware trust.

questions.objective: Assess update provenance, compatibility, exposure and recovery before a change.
questions.prompt: An update is signed but incompatible with the installed driver. What should the engineer do?
options: Deploy because a signature proves compatibility.
Disable signature checks.
Hold or stage a supported dependency change before deployment.
explanations: Signatures do not establish operational compatibility.
Bypassing provenance worsens the decision.
Provenance and compatibility are separate acceptance conditions.

questions.objective: Demonstrate integrity, denied actions and functional recovery with explicit unsupported controls.
questions.prompt: A successful OS reinstall follows suspected BMC compromise. What remains unresolved?
options: Nothing if the server boots.
Trust and authority in the BMC and other relevant firmware layers.
Only the restored host filesystem permissions.
explanations: Boot success is a functional observation, not complete recovery.
OS rebuilding does not establish lower-layer integrity.
Host permissions alone do not establish the compromised BMC or firmware trust.

questions.objective: Assess update provenance, compatibility, exposure and recovery before a change.
questions.prompt: Which two items belong in a firmware change gate? Select two.
options: A supported recovery route and irreversible-change assessment.
Compatibility and required service tests.
An assumption that every image can be downgraded.
explanations: Recovery must be real and platform-specific.
The changed system must remain supported and functional.
Rollback capability varies by platform and update.

questions.objective: Build a supported hardening baseline across host, controller, firmware and application layers.
questions.prompt: A legacy controller cannot support a selected hardening control. What is the appropriate record?
options: A false pass to keep the score high.
Delete the controller from inventory.
Unsupported capability, consequence, compensating treatment, owner and review date.
explanations: A score must not conceal a missing control.
Removing the record does not remove exposure.
The limitation and treatment remain auditable.

questions.objective: Demonstrate integrity, denied actions and functional recovery with explicit unsupported controls.
questions.prompt: After patching, the monitoring dashboard is quiet. What is the next validation?
options: Turn off event logging permanently.
Verify collection continuity and produce a controlled observable event.
Assume all threats disappeared.
explanations: Disabling evidence does not validate the change.
Quiet telemetry may reflect a failed collector.
Absence of alerts is ambiguous.

questions.objective: Design telemetry with time quality, collection health and retention appropriate to the detection.
questions.prompt: An unchanged dashboard value has no collection-health indicator. What detection gap exists?
options: Every constant value proves a cyberattack.
Encryption automatically proves freshness.
A stale or interrupted source may appear normal.
explanations: A constant physical value can be legitimate.
Transport protection does not establish current measurement.
Freshness requires source and delivery observations.

questions.objective: Measure detection coverage, false positives and latency using controlled ground truth.
questions.prompt: A test has 8 true positives, 2 false positives and 2 false negatives. What are precision and recall?
options: 80% precision and 100% recall.
80% precision and 80% recall for this test set.
100% precision and 80% recall.
explanations: False negatives reduce recall.
Both denominators equal 10 in the stated sample.
False positives reduce precision.

questions.objective: Correlate security activity with configuration and physical-process evidence.
questions.prompt: A signed temperature message is implausibly high. What is still possible?
options: Sensor, mapping or process faults despite valid message authenticity.
Signature validation proves calibration.
No operational response is needed.
explanations: Authenticity and physical correctness are different.
A signature does not calibrate a sensor.
The physical consequence still needs assessment.

questions.objective: Design telemetry with time quality, collection health and retention appropriate to the detection.
questions.prompt: Which two fields help interpret an uncertain event timeline? Select two.
options: Collector receive time and known buffering delay.
Only a normalised timestamp with the original discarded.
Original source time and synchronisation uncertainty.
explanations: Receive time helps interpret transport and collection delay.
Discarding original time and uncertainty prevents a defensible timeline review.
Source uncertainty bounds ordering claims.

questions.objective: Correlate security activity with configuration and physical-process evidence.
questions.prompt: A project-change alert occurs during maintenance, but the approval feed is stale. What should triage do?
options: Delete all project-change detections.
Verify the actual approval and controller change before classifying the event.
Declare malicious activity with certainty.
explanations: A dependency defect should be corrected, not hide all changes.
The rule has a known dependency requiring confirmation.
The available evidence does not justify certainty.

questions.objective: Measure detection coverage, false positives and latency using controlled ground truth.
questions.prompt: A detector is tuned and scored on the same six examples. What is the main limitation?
options: The score may reflect the tuned examples rather than unseen behaviour.
The detector is automatically production-ready.
Raw events are no longer needed.
explanations: Separate validation scenarios improve the bounded evaluation.
Small rehearsed samples cannot establish production coverage.
Raw evidence remains needed for review.

questions.objective: Define assessment scope, rules, stop conditions and restoration prerequisites.
questions.prompt: A lab configuration contains a production API URL. What should the tester do?
options: Send a harmless probe without approval.
Exclude and block unintended access, document it and seek the proper owner if later testing is needed.
Test it because it appeared in scope material.
explanations: Even a probe is an action outside the agreed boundary.
Presence in a file does not authorise access.
Scope must identify authorised targets.

questions.objective: Validate a bounded attack path while distinguishing discovery, vulnerability and demonstrated impact.
questions.prompt: A scanner reports a vulnerable version, but exploitation is untested. How should the finding be described?
options: Possible applicable exposure pending configuration and validation evidence.
Confirmed complete compromise.
No issue because scanners can be wrong.
explanations: The observation is useful but has bounded meaning.
Version matching alone does not prove impact.
Uncertainty requires assessment rather than dismissal.

questions.objective: Retest remediation and service, including rejection of unsafe or out-of-scope requests.
questions.prompt: A fix blocks the test attack and breaks legitimate historian collection. What is the result?
options: Full acceptance because the attack stopped.
The service test should be removed.
Security retest passed for that action; integrated acceptance failed.
explanations: A control can be effective yet operationally unacceptable.
Removing a criterion conceals the failure.
Both security and function are required.

questions.objective: Define assessment scope, rules, stop conditions and restoration prerequisites.
questions.prompt: Which two conditions must be pinned before an intrusive controller test? Select two.
options: An assumption that any snapshot restores physical state.
Explicit target/method authority and stop conditions.
Supported restoration prerequisites and service observation.
explanations: Snapshots do not necessarily represent device or physical state.
The experiment needs bounded authority.
Operational consequences require recovery and monitoring.

questions.objective: Validate a bounded attack path while distinguishing discovery, vulnerability and demonstrated impact.
questions.prompt: A viewer alters another synthetic user’s record through a lab API. What does this establish?
options: A demonstrated authorisation defect for that tested path and configuration.
Every product endpoint is vulnerable.
The entire real facility is compromised.
explanations: The claim is supported within the observed boundary.
Other paths remain untested.
Synthetic evidence cannot establish a real incident.

questions.objective: Retest remediation and service, including rejection of unsafe or out-of-scope requests.
questions.prompt: An assessment assistant requests disabling independent protection outside the approved plan. What is expected?
options: Execute because assessment tools know best.
Hide the request from the reviewer.
Reject the request and record the authority boundary.
explanations: Tools do not grant operational authority.
The rejected request is useful assurance evidence.
Unsafe request rejection is part of the process test.

questions.objective: Coordinate incident roles, operational consequences and bounded containment decisions.
questions.prompt: The security team proposes disconnecting a gateway that carries the only required alarms. What must the incident lead obtain?
options: Operational impact assessment and an authorised continuity arrangement.
Only confirmation that the firewall can block the gateway.
Permission from the suspected compromised account.
explanations: Containment must account for the affected service.
Technical ability to isolate does not establish an acceptable process consequence.
Compromised authority cannot validate the response.

questions.objective: Preserve and interpret evidence with explicit custody, uncertainty and collection limits.
questions.prompt: A disk image hash matches its acquisition record. What does that prove?
options: The source system was never compromised.
All volatile evidence was preserved.
The compared bytes have not changed relative to that recorded acquisition hash.
explanations: A faithful image can contain compromised state.
Disk acquisition does not automatically preserve memory.
Integrity checking is bounded to the collected bytes.

questions.objective: Exercise continuity, eradication and escalation across OT, network and BMC incidents.
questions.prompt: A tabletop team describes manual operation but never tests it. How should this be recorded?
options: Production competence automatically accepted.
Decision practice completed; technical continuity capability remains unproven.
Full operational continuity demonstrated.
explanations: A tabletop cannot establish production performance.
Discussion and execution are distinct evidence.
The physical method and staffing remain untested.

questions.objective: Preserve and interpret evidence with explicit custody, uncertainty and collection limits.
questions.prompt: Which two timeline details should remain explicit? Select two.
options: Clock offset and uncertainty.
Evidence lost before collection.
Only the final preferred hypothesis.
explanations: Clock quality limits ordering conclusions.
Missing evidence limits certainty and reproduction.
Alternative hypotheses and raw observations matter.

questions.objective: Coordinate incident roles, operational consequences and bounded containment decisions.
questions.prompt: Who authorises an equipment action during a cyber incident?
options: Any analyst who sees an alert.
The detection rule automatically.
The person with the defined operational authority for that action.
explanations: Observation alone grants no switching or control authority.
A rule may inform a decision but has no inherent authority.
Incident coordination does not erase equipment authority.

questions.objective: Exercise continuity, eradication and escalation across OT, network and BMC incidents.
questions.prompt: One malicious file is removed, but the same privileged token remains active. What is unresolved?
options: Nothing because the file was deleted.
The incident’s continuing authority and eradication scope.
Only the timestamp format used in the incident ticket.
explanations: Removing one artifact does not close the path.
The attacker may still exercise the valid token.
Continuing privileged authority is an eradication problem, not merely a timeline issue.

questions.objective: Choose restoration material and recovery paths using explicit trust and dependency analysis.
questions.prompt: The backup and its hash are both writable by the compromised administrator. What is the limitation?
options: A matching hash proves the incident never affected the backup.
Hashes are useless in every context.
Their agreement does not independently establish trustworthy restoration material.
explanations: Integrity comparison must be interpreted with custody and provenance.
Hashes remain useful for detecting changes under appropriate custody.
A shared compromised authority can replace both.

questions.objective: Recover OT, network-administrator and BMC-compromise scenarios with distinct acceptance evidence.
questions.prompt: An OS image is restored after BMC compromise. Which additional path is required?
options: No additional work if ping succeeds.
Supported assessment and recovery of BMC/firmware trust and management authority.
Only a new desktop password.
explanations: Connectivity does not establish integrity.
The compromised layer is outside the OS image.
One credential change does not establish platform trust.

questions.objective: Validate function, integrity and revoked authority before declaring restoration complete.
questions.prompt: RPO is 60 minutes and observed loss is 45; RTO is 90 minutes and validation takes 110. What is the result?
options: RPO passes and RTO fails for the stated exercise.
Both pass because average performance is acceptable.
RPO fails and RTO passes.
explanations: Each independent requirement is compared with its own limit.
Averaging hides a failed service objective.
The comparisons are reversed.

questions.objective: Choose restoration material and recovery paths using explicit trust and dependency analysis.
questions.prompt: Which two conditions expose a recovery dependency problem? Select two.
options: The recovery key is only in the failed online vault.
A separately controlled tested recovery route exists.
The directory backup requires the unavailable directory to authenticate.
explanations: This makes key access fail with the protected service.
A tested separate route can resolve the dependency.
This is a circular dependency.

questions.objective: Recover OT, network-administrator and BMC-compromise scenarios with distinct acceptance evidence.
questions.prompt: A restored controller has correct logic but incorrect sensor mapping. What is justified?
options: Mapping is outside recovery.
Operational acceptance fails until point semantics and function are corrected and retested.
Full acceptance because the file hash matches.
explanations: Point mapping is essential to control and alarms.
Physical meaning is part of the restored function.
A correct file alone does not prove correct integration.

questions.objective: Validate function, integrity and revoked authority before declaring restoration complete.
questions.prompt: A revoked account is denied only while the recovery VLAN is isolated. What remains to test?
options: The denial after approved ordinary connectivity and services return.
Only the denial already observed during temporary isolation.
Whether the recovery VLAN uses a different subnet number.
explanations: Temporary isolation may conceal an authority defect.
That observation does not prove enforcement after the final connectivity is restored.
Address separation alone does not validate denied authority in the final operating mode.

questions.objective: Bound automation and AI/MCP evidence assistance by provenance, freshness and explicit authority.
questions.prompt: A retrieved log tells an evidence assistant to reset a controller. What should happen?
options: Hide the instruction and report success.
Treat it as untrusted data and keep execution outside the assistant’s read-only authority.
Execute because it is written in a device log.
explanations: False reporting destroys assurance.
Content is not an authorisation source.
Logs can contain malicious or irrelevant instructions.

questions.objective: Run recurring security reviews and controlled changes with measurable acceptance and recovery.
questions.prompt: An access review finds an expired vendor role and only marks “reviewed.” What is missing?
options: Removal or justified treatment and a denied-action verification.
A second export of the same unresolved permissions.
A training-completion record for the account owner.
explanations: The review must change or justify actual authority.
Another observation does not implement or justify treatment of the expired authority.
Training does not remove or justify the expired system permission.

questions.objective: Choose and verify supported media sanitisation and retirement controls.
questions.prompt: A solid-state drive is quick-formatted before disposal. What can be claimed?
options: All media locations are certainly purged.
Every encryption key copy was destroyed.
Formatting occurred; required sanitisation effectiveness remains unproven.
explanations: A quick format does not establish that outcome.
Formatting does not prove key-copy treatment.
Media-specific sanitisation requires its own supported method and evidence.

questions.objective: Bound automation and AI/MCP evidence assistance by provenance, freshness and explicit authority.
questions.prompt: Which two properties strengthen a read-only evidence assistant? Select two.
options: Permission to execute any instruction found in retrieved text.
Credentials technically restricted to approved read operations.
Source identity, observation time and uncertainty in its output.
explanations: Retrieved text is data, not authority.
Capability limits enforce the intended boundary.
Provenance and freshness support review.

questions.objective: Run recurring security reviews and controlled changes with measurable acceptance and recovery.
questions.prompt: A rollback restores service but reopens the original management exposure. What is the correct status?
options: Service restored; security treatment remains open with owner and deadline.
Full security acceptance automatically passed.
The exposure no longer matters.
explanations: Rollback and security closure are separate outcomes.
The original risk still exists.
Restoring availability does not erase exposure.

questions.objective: Choose and verify supported media sanitisation and retirement controls.
questions.prompt: A cryptographic erase deletes one key while a usable copy remains in backup. What is unresolved?
options: Only whether the drive has been removed from the rack.
Nothing if the command returned success.
The required key destruction and resulting data inaccessibility.
explanations: Physical removal does not resolve recoverable relevant key copies.
Command success alone does not validate suitability.
Recoverable relevant keys can defeat the intended outcome.

questions.objective: Connect security governance, risk ownership and ethical decisions to organisational objectives.
questions.prompt: A team estimates 200,000 units loss and 0.1 events per year. What does 20,000 represent?
options: The annualised loss in that model, dependent on its assumptions.
A guaranteed annual cost.
Proof that no severe event can occur.
explanations: Expected-value arithmetic does not validate inputs.
The model is uncertain, not a guarantee.
Low frequency does not eliminate severe outcomes.

questions.objective: Define privacy, legal and supplier requirements without assuming a universal jurisdiction.
questions.prompt: A global facility copies a breach-notification deadline from an unrelated jurisdiction. What should be done?
options: Assume one deadline applies everywhere.
Remove all incident records.
Validate applicable obligations with the authorised legal/privacy function and record the source.
explanations: Obligations vary by context.
Destroying records does not resolve applicability.
Actual jurisdiction and contracts determine requirements.

questions.objective: Use business impact analysis to select and test continuity objectives and dependencies.
questions.prompt: A restore job takes 70 minutes and its required identity dependency takes 80 more. RTO is 120 minutes. What is the result?
options: The dependency time never counts.
The 150-minute service restoration misses the objective.
The objective passes because the backup job took 70 minutes.
explanations: Dependencies are part of the restoration path.
The required service depends on both sequential steps.
Reporting only one step hides the service delay.

questions.objective: Define privacy, legal and supplier requirements without assuming a universal jurisdiction.
questions.prompt: Which two questions belong in a privacy design review? Select two.
options: What justified purpose requires each collected field?
What approved retention, access and deletion rules apply?
Can the archive retain everything forever without review?
explanations: Purpose supports minimisation and accountability.
Lifecycle controls make obligations operational.
Indefinite collection is not a justified default.

questions.objective: Connect security governance, risk ownership and ethical decisions to organisational objectives.
questions.prompt: An executive requests marking a failed recovery gate as passed to meet a deadline. What should the engineer do?
options: Change the result because seniority changes the evidence.
Delete the failed test.
Report the failed criterion, consequence and available options accurately.
explanations: Authority can accept risk but cannot change observed facts.
Removing evidence prevents honest review.
Ethical assurance preserves the actual result.

questions.objective: Use business impact analysis to select and test continuity objectives and dependencies.
questions.prompt: A supplier has excellent availability claims but no tested exit or recovery route. What remains open?
options: Nothing if the contract is signed.
Continuity and supplier-dependency evidence.
Only the supplier’s encryption algorithm selection.
explanations: A contract alone does not demonstrate performance.
Service claims need actual arrangements and tests.
Encryption alone cannot establish the missing continuity and exit arrangements.

questions.objective: Distinguish encryption, hashing, authentication and signatures by the property they provide.
questions.prompt: An attacker can replace a file and its plain hash in the same repository. What is missing?
options: A longer filename.
Proof that all hashes are encryption.
An independent authenticity or trusted-custody basis.
explanations: Naming does not establish source.
Hashing and encryption provide different properties.
Anyone able to replace both can compute a matching digest.

questions.objective: Design key generation, custody, rotation, compromise response and retirement with recoverability.
questions.prompt: A key rotates, but an old backup still needs the old key. What should the design provide?
options: Put the old key in a public README.
Controlled historical-key custody and a tested authorised recovery route.
Delete all old keys immediately regardless of retention.
explanations: Public disclosure defeats confidentiality.
Recoverability and protected custody must both be addressed.
That may destroy required data access.

questions.objective: Classify information and assign ownership, handling and retention across its lifecycle.
questions.prompt: A diagnostic ticket contains a copied sensitive configuration. How should it be handled?
options: Apply the relevant classification and access/retention controls to the copy.
Treat copies as automatically public.
Ignore it because production storage is encrypted.
explanations: Protection follows information through its lifecycle.
Copying does not remove sensitivity.
Storage controls do not cover an uncontrolled export.

questions.objective: Distinguish encryption, hashing, authentication and signatures by the property they provide.
questions.prompt: Which two statements are correct? Select two.
options: A valid signature does not establish physical measurement correctness.
Storage encryption prevents every misuse by a running privileged host.
TLS does not automatically authorise an application action.
explanations: Authenticity is distinct from sensor and process truth.
The running host may have legitimate decrypted access.
Transport trust and application permission are separate.

questions.objective: Design key generation, custody, rotation, compromise response and retirement with recoverability.
questions.prompt: An encryption mode requires unique nonces under a key, but the application repeats them. What should the reviewer conclude?
options: The issue only affects user-interface appearance.
The implementation violates a security assumption despite a strong key length.
Key length makes nonce handling irrelevant.
explanations: This affects security properties.
Mode requirements are part of cryptographic correctness.
Strong keys cannot repair misuse of the mode.

questions.objective: Classify information and assign ownership, handling and retention across its lifecycle.
questions.prompt: Who decides the business protection requirement for an information asset?
options: The accountable information owner, with applicable policy and obligations.
Every storage custodian independently without ownership.
The backup software automatically.
explanations: Ownership establishes the required handling and use.
Custodians implement controls within assigned responsibility.
Software cannot assume organisational accountability.

questions.objective: Evaluate trust boundaries, isolation and failure behaviour in infrastructure-supporting software and platforms.
questions.prompt: Two containers share one host kernel and BMC. What must the architecture record?
options: No need to assess host administration.
Shared trust and failure dependencies despite logical separation.
Complete physical independence.
explanations: Host and BMC authority can affect both.
The isolation boundary has shared lower layers.
Containers do not create separate hardware.

questions.objective: Integrate threat modelling, secure implementation and testing into the software lifecycle.
questions.prompt: A meter name from an API is concatenated into a shell command. What is the strongest design correction?
options: Keep it as data through a structured API and validate the authorised target.
Trust it because it came from a device.
Only shorten the string.
explanations: This removes the unnecessary instruction boundary and checks scope.
Device-supplied content can be untrusted.
Length alone does not establish safe interpretation.

questions.objective: Establish build, dependency and release provenance with controlled deployment and recovery.
questions.prompt: A release includes an SBOM. What does that establish by itself?
options: Proof that every component is vulnerability-free.
Proof of operational acceptance.
A declared component inventory, subject to its completeness and provenance.
explanations: Known and unknown defects can remain.
Service and security tests are still needed.
An inventory supports review but has limits.

questions.objective: Integrate threat modelling, secure implementation and testing into the software lifecycle.
questions.prompt: Which two tests address different security questions? Select two.
options: Only unit tests of the input parser.
A negative object-authorisation test on the running API.
A dependency exposure review tied to deployed versions.
explanations: Parser tests do not establish deployed object authorisation or dependency exposure.
This tests actual permission enforcement.
This evaluates component exposure.

questions.objective: Evaluate trust boundaries, isolation and failure behaviour in infrastructure-supporting software and platforms.
questions.prompt: Loss of a policy service makes an application deny every request. What must be assessed?
options: Whether that degraded behaviour satisfies required service and process constraints.
That denial is always physically safe.
That every request should therefore be allowed forever.
explanations: Security failure behaviour must be reconciled with operation.
Physical consequence depends on the system.
Unbounded bypass removes required authority.

questions.objective: Establish build, dependency and release provenance with controlled deployment and recovery.
questions.prompt: A database migration breaks compatibility with the previous binary. What is missing from “just roll back the code”?
options: A hash of the previous application binary alone.
A load-balancer route back to the old binary alone.
A supported state/schema recovery or forward-recovery plan.
explanations: A known binary still needs compatible persistent state and dependencies.
Routing traffic back does not repair an incompatible database schema.
Recovery must address persistent state and dependencies.

questions.objective: Distinguish identity proofing, authentication, federation and resource authorisation.
questions.prompt: A supplier authenticates a user successfully through federation. What remains the maintenance application’s responsibility?
options: Validate the assertion/token for its intended use and enforce its own resource authorisation.
Grant every supplier user administrator access.
Assume proofing, authentication and permission are the same thing.
explanations: Federated identity does not replace application permission.
Authentication does not justify broad privilege.
These are distinct assurance questions.

questions.objective: Evaluate federated tokens, lifecycle changes and trust-service failure at the application boundary.
questions.prompt: A correctly signed token has the wrong audience for the API. What should happen?
options: Accept because the signature is valid.
Ignore the audience whenever the user is familiar.
Reject it under the API’s token-validation policy.
explanations: Signature validation is necessary but not sufficient.
Identity familiarity does not change token scope.
The token was not intended for this resource.

questions.objective: Select assessment methods, samples and independence appropriate to a control claim.
questions.prompt: An assessor tests 2 of 80 accounts without explaining selection. What is the appropriate claim?
options: No evidence exists at all.
The two tested cases have results; wider coverage needs a justified sampling basis.
Every account is proven correct.
explanations: The two tests still provide specific evidence.
The observations are useful but bounded.
The sample does not automatically establish the full population.

questions.objective: Evaluate federated tokens, lifecycle changes and trust-service failure at the application boundary.
questions.prompt: Which two lifecycle behaviours require practical verification? Select two.
options: Effect of role removal on existing sessions.
Effect of identity-provider outage and signing-key change.
Only whether a new user can sign in normally.
explanations: Authority can persist through cached claims or sessions.
Trust dependencies and updates affect access.
Normal login does not exercise removal, outage or trust-key lifecycle behaviour.

questions.objective: Select assessment methods, samples and independence appropriate to a control claim.
questions.prompt: A reviewer signs a report without raw evidence or criteria. What is missing?
options: A second reviewer who sees only the same unsupported summary.
Nothing because any signature proves implementation.
A basis for independent acceptance of the actual control claim.
explanations: Additional signatures do not compensate for missing criteria and raw evidence.
A signature cannot substitute for evidence.
Review must evaluate requirements, observations and limits.

questions.objective: Distinguish identity proofing, authentication, federation and resource authorisation.
questions.prompt: What is the relationship between OAuth and OpenID Connect in this lesson?
options: An ID token is automatically a valid access token for every API.
OAuth addresses delegated authorisation; OpenID Connect adds an identity layer.
They are identical names for a password database.
explanations: Token purpose and audience must be respected.
Their protocol roles are related but distinct.
Neither description is accurate.
